ety.text: From Middle English or; partially contracted from other, auther, from Old English āþor, āwþer, āhwæþer ("some, any, either"; > either); and partially from Middle English oththe, from Old English oþþe, from Proto-Germanic *efþau (“or”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian of (“or”), Cimbrian odar, òdar (“or”), Dutch of, oft, ofte (“or”), German, Luxembourgish, and Vilamovian oder (“or”), Low German of, àder, àr, åder, år (“or”), Yiddish אָדער (oder, “or”), Icelandic eða, eður (“or”), Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau, “or; otherwise”).
From late Middle English or (“gold”), borrowed from Middle French or (“yellow”), from Old French or, from Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of aurum.
From Late Old English ār, from Old Norse ár. Compare ere.

senses.d: Connects at least two alternative words, phrases, clauses, sentences, etc., each of which could make a passage true.
ex: He might get cancer, or be hit by a bus, or God knows what.

senses.d: An operator denoting the disjunction of two propositions or truth values. There are two forms: the inclusive or and the exclusive or.
Counts the elements before and after as two possibilities.
Otherwise (a consequence of the condition that the previous is false).
ex: It's raining! Come inside or you'll catch a cold!

senses.d: Used in between two numbers to denote a range between them.
The gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.
ex: The metals are gold and silver, these being termed "or" and "argent".
In engraving, "Or" is expressed by dots.

senses.d: Of gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.
Before; ere. Generally followed by “ever” or “e'er”.
ex:
I looked to heaven, and tried to pray;
But or ever a prayer had gusht,
A wicked whisper came, and made
My heart as dry as dust.
